output.headline: Burnham to unveil publicly owned body to speed up grid connections
output.bodyHtml:
Andy Burnham will take his first major step towards putting Britain’s utility companies into public control when he announces a new government-backed body to invest in the electricity grid at the Labour conference.

The prime minister will use his first speech as party leader to announce the creation of GB Grid, which will use money previously allocated to Great British Energy to compete with privately owned companies such as National Grid.

In a speech focusing heavily on undoing what the prime minister calls ‘40 years of neoliberalism’, he will promise greater public control of energy, water and housing.

He is also set to lay out more details on how he will pay for his pledge to create a national care service, with senior ministers refusing to rule out scrapping the pensions triple lock after the next election to free funding.

Government sources have suggested Burnham would signal his willingness to review the policy, but stop short of a pledge to scrap it altogether.

Burnham will tell the conference on Tuesday: ‘We have a cost crisis. We all know it. The price of energy is crippling for businesses, and British bill payers pay some of the highest energy costs in Europe.

‘We have an energy system where prices are dictated in markets miles away, while families and businesses here shoulder the costs. Once again, the British public has lost control.’

He will add: ‘Within 10 years, I want our energy costs to be in line with other nations in Europe. That means we must reform a broken energy market so it serves the public interest.’

Burnham’s first conference speech as leader and prime minister caps a remarkable turnaround in his political fortunes since this time last year, when he was criticised by many in the party for talking openly about his desire to replace Keir Starmer.

Having ousted Starmer from office, Burnham has spent much of his first few weeks promising a radical shift in tone and policy.

He will tell the conference on Tuesday: ‘We can’t carry on as we are. Politics as usual has taken Britain backwards. More of the same isn’t good enough and isn’t going to get us where we need to be.’

Though the conference has been upbeat, Burnham will tell Labour delegates he wanted to strike a serious tone with his speech and address some of the most intractable issues in British politics, such as social care, energy costs and youth inactivity.

In the speech, the prime minister will say that he will resist ‘the usual tub-thumping conference speech … the patriot in me tells me something very different is needed’.

He will say ‘everyone wants less drift and more direction’ and that he will ‘answer that call’ today. His offer – expected to contain a number of new policies – will be ‘a more serious prospectus for Britain than people have been offered in a generation’.

‘I accept people will not agree with every part of it, but I believe it can turn Britain around,’ he will say.

GB Grid will be his first significant step to challenging the power of private companies to run Britain’s infrastructure.

The organisation will be given access to a pot of £4bn that has already been allocated to the government-backed Great British Energy – although it is not expected to use all of that money.

GB Grid will use the funding to build more connections and to maximise and speed up the rollout of renewables across the UK, addressing businesses’ complaints about how long it takes to get a grid connection for new buildings and projects. It will be the first publicly owned player in electricity networks since privatisation.

Officials said the government would also expand the rights of businesses to build their own connections, allowing them to tap GB Grid’s funding to help pay for it – a move which they said helped speed up connections in Ireland by 11 months.

Speaking to the Guardian’s Politics Weekly podcast on Monday, the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, said: ‘One of my frustrations with the last government is that they didn’t recognise the need to invest in the system, and so we’re having to do that at record pace over the course of the next decade.’

On social care, the prime minister will promise ‘an honest conversation’ with the public, saying: ‘Hope comes from honesty and from saying the things politicians usually avoid.’

His promise to ‘rip the plaster off’ when it comes to funding for the national care service has sparked speculation he could use the next Labour manifesto to scrap the pension triple lock and use the savings for social care instead.

The triple lock – which guarantees the state pension will rise by the highest of inflation, earnings and 2.5% every year – is forecast to cost £15.5bn by 2030, but so far no major party has remained committed to scrapping it.

Speaking to ITV’s Robert Peston on Monday, the chancellor, John Healey, repeatedly refused to commit to funding the triple lock beyond the next election.

‘I’m not telling you what the next manifesto will or won’t contain – I can’t do that,’ he said. ‘I’m not going to tell you what the budget in a month’s time is going to take.’

The prime minister is also set to talk about youth unemployment ahead of a planned report by former minister Alan Milburn on why the number of unemployed young people is rising.

The government has already announced additional support for young people to get into work, though ministers have said relatively little about whether they will reduce benefits for those who remain out of work in the long term.

Answering calls on LBC Radio on Monday, Burnham said he would use his speech to outline ‘how I think we should go forward in the next decade’.

‘It will require some significant changes, but I’m doing it with the best of intentions,’ he said.
output.standfirst: Exclusive: Andy Burnham will tell Labour’s conference that GB Grid, a new publicly backed body with access to a £4bn pot, will speed up grid connections as he vows to tackle Britain’s high energy bills.
output.progress: Burnham is set to create GB Grid, a publicly backed body that will get access to £4bn to speed up grid connections.

output.headline: Investigators find no explosives in RAF Fairford bomb plot probe
output.bodyHtml:
No explosive material had been found, it emerged after the suspects’ release, following an initial examination of the vans that had led police to suspect they carried explosives and to assess whether they were viable improvised explosive devices.

Detectives believe it is unlikely the men were on the brink of a mass casualty attack by exploding a bomb close to the base, sources said, a judgment reflected in their release on police bail.

Five suspects arrested close to the RAF Fairford airbase were released on bail hours before the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said unequivocally that a foreign actor was involved in the suspected UK bomb plot.

Related: Questions remain over Iran’s link to alleged RAF Fairford bomb plot

A local farmer alerted police to three white vans driving towards RAF Fairford, a British base that houses US bombers that fly missions against Iran, leading to the early Sunday detention of the five men, all British nationals from London in their early 20s.

They were arrested on suspicion of explosives offences and preparing an act of terrorism, with an Iranian link a key line of inquiry.

Rubio thanked the British authorities for their handling of the incident, while also saying a lot of people were “disturbed that some of these people [being investigated] have been released on bail”.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said in July the base was a legitimate target. Iran’s embassy in London has denied any involvement in the events near RAF Fairford.

Rubio provided no evidence for his claims.

Earlier in the day, Donald Trump told reporters at the White House on Monday that he would not have released the suspects on bail. “We know everything about them. We would not have released them.”

Asked whether the case was linked to Iran, Trump said: “It might be.”

Pressed to give details, Trump said: “I’d rather not. I mean I know the answer, I could be very specific, but I’d rather not say. I would not have released them.”

British sources have suggested the specific activities of the men were unknown, though Trump has previously suggested the plot was known to the US authorities.

The head of UK counter-terrorism policing, the assistant commissioner Laurence Taylor, said the release of the men on bail did not mean the investigation was over and that they were subject to “stringent conditions”.

He said: “I know there is significant interest in whether the current geopolitical context has a bearing on this incident. At counter-terrorism policing we are working within this context every day, and at this stage we are keeping an open mind in this investigation.

“… But be assured, we are considering this from every possible angle. Including, that this may be activity committed by proxies, or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly working on behalf of a foreign state.”

“What could have happened in the UK over the weekend is a very serious situation,” Rubio said in an interview with Fox News on Monday evening, adding that it “clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor.”

Iran is suspected of using proxies in the UK, in incidents ranging from alleged arson attacks against Jewish targets to men flying a basic drone near the Israeli embassy.
output.standfirst: No explosive material had been found and detectives thought a mass-casualty attack unlikely, though Marco Rubio said, without evidence, that a foreign actor was involved and many were ‘disturbed’ the suspects had been bailed.
output.progress: UK counter-terrorism police are keeping an open mind and considering every angle, with the five suspects under stringent bail conditions.

output.headline: Angela Rayner backs lifeboat volunteers targeted by online hatred
output.bodyHtml:
Angela Rayner, the communities secretary, said she was deeply concerned by the way social media was amplifying extreme voices – especially those targeting the RNLI.

She said far-right marches led by the self-styled “Danny Tommo” should not be treated like normal protests, calling the marches “intimidation” that should not be permitted.

Daniel Thomas, the instigator of the marches over the past month, was arrested and charged last week after allegedly using a blade to slash an inflatable dinghy in the Channel while a rescue worker was onboard.

Rayner said the behaviour of some masked marchers – who have blocked roads and transport hubs – was not an acceptable form of protest.

Rayner said the marches were frightening local people. “When you see hundreds of predominantly men in black wearing black face masks shouting, going down the street, that is intimidating,” she said. “Whether you agree with the message or not, it’s intimidating.”

She added: “It is not a protest. I’ve been on many protests myself when I was in my union days. We have music, we have banners, but we don’t wear balaclavas and shout divisive rhetoric down the street.

“There’s a line, and I think organising to disrupt and cordon off areas to stop people going through public highways, this is all behaviour that is intimidatory and is not acceptable.”

Thomas has recently brought dozens of nationalist protest groups together under the umbrella name of Patriot Platform. Masked and hooded anti-migrant activists from the movement have convened in English coastal towns and ports, in one case blocking traffic in and out of the port of Dover.

On the day that a 10-year-old child and two women died ⁠attempting ​to cross the Channel, Rayner said there needed to be more humanity about how migrants were described and treated when they attempted to cross in small boats.

“How can we get to the point where we dehumanise like this,” she asked. “Yes, we can have an argument about the criminals putting people on these boats, the legitimacy of someone’s claim. But when you’ve got a human being at risk of death, do we let them drown?

“That is ultimately what it comes down to. Yes, we politicians have a discussion about policies, about people we give asylum to, about how we stop boats. But [to] attack volunteers that save people from drowning?

“These are volunteers. If there’s a risk to life at sea, an RNLI volunteer without any political persuasion at all or any ideology will go out and will save lives at sea.

“To whip up hatred as if they are making a judgment on the value of these lives that they’re saving or not, and to put their faces up, identify them, to whip up online hatred towards volunteers whose sole job is to give up their time to save lives at sea. It’s not acceptable.”
output.standfirst: Angela Rayner defended RNLI volunteers being targeted with online hatred, as she condemned marches by ‘men in black wearing face masks’ as intimidatory and unacceptable.
output.progress: Angela Rayner is condemning intimidatory far-right marches and hate campaigns against RNLI volunteers, while police have already charged march instigator Daniel Thomas.

output.headline: Study finds screen time's impact on children rivals other key factors
output.bodyHtml:
Some experts have urged caution over how the findings of a major new study on children’s screen time should be read, arguing they in no way support the idea that screens are the main cause of adolescent distress.

Tatiana Íñiguez Berrozpe, a senior lecturer in sociology at the University of Zaragoza in Spain, said the report showed an association between screen time and poorer mental health and academic performance, but that it was small.

‘This is not an insignificant finding, but it in no way supports the mantra that screens are the main cause of adolescent emotional distress,’ she said. ‘Screen use alone does not explain why a teenager is emotionally distressed or performs less well academically.’

Esther van Sluijs, a professor of behavioural epidemiology at Loughborough University, said the study was ‘high-quality’ but could not differentiate between different types of screen use.

‘It cannot draw robust conclusions about specific types of screen use, like social media use or gaming, as there was not enough data to study this. We should therefore be cautious in interpreting these results in the context of young people’s current screen use habits,’ she said.

The effect of high screen time on children is as significant as parental behaviour and premature birth, if not greater, a global study has found.

Researchers examined data on more than 2.8 million children across 64 countries and concluded that elevated screen exposure could affect children in areas including academic achievement and emotional problems. It is one of the largest ever studies on the subject.

The impacts are ‘similar in magnitude to or larger’ than other factors linked to child development and mental health outcomes including family wealth, the behaviour of parents and whether or not children were born prematurely.

Higher screen use for gaming, social media and streaming can lead to lower academic achievement and language development issues, the study suggests.

Researchers found in the review, published in the journal JAMA Pediatrics, that children who spend more time on screens have higher ‘socioemotional’ and mental health problems. Academics conducted a so-called umbrella review, which summarises results from previous large reviews on the topic.

Related: Time limits, curfews or a full ban: how UK may restrict social media for under-16s

Researchers found that longer durations of digital and social media use were linked to ‘less favourable outcomes across multiple (although not all) measured domains of children’s developmental health’. The analysis covered a variety of devices, from smartphones to televisions, and a range of activities including scrolling social media, gaming and FaceTime calls.

‘Together, the findings suggest that screen use may represent one potentially modifiable factor associated with children’s wellbeing across multiple domains,’ the report said.

It found that greater screen exposure was associated with overall lower grades at school. When academics examined specific subjects, screen time did not appear to be linked to maths, reading or science attainment, but the researchers said these were ‘among the least studied’, so the finding may be due to a lack of evidence.

The researchers, led by academics at the University of Calgary in Canada, did find that higher screen time was also linked to poorer language development.

When they looked at mental health, they found that higher screen use was linked to emotional and ‘peer problems’; ‘internalising behaviour’, which includes symptoms of depression and anxiety; and externalising behaviour, including aggression and attention deficit hyperactivity disorder symptoms.

‘Our review revealed that higher so-called doses of screen exposure are associated with lower overall academic achievement and poorer language development, as well as higher internalising and externalising behaviour, emotional problems and peer problems,’ the authors wrote.

‘Notably, these effect sizes are similar in magnitude to or larger than those reported for other well-established predictors of children’s outcomes, such as socioeconomic status, parenting behaviour and preterm birth.’

Additional reporting by Press Association
output.standfirst: One expert cautions against reading a major study as proof that screens are the main cause of children's distress, though its findings on learning and emotional health rival those of parental behaviour and premature birth.

output.headline: Premier League rivals step up calls to publish Manchester City verdict
output.bodyHtml:
Premier League clubs are pushing for the Manchester City verdict to be published as soon as possible, while the club digs in for a long battle to clear its name.

Manchester City’s chief executive, Ferran Soriano, told a meeting of the European Football Clubs board on Monday that the club will fight to prove its innocence after being found guilty by an independent commission of the vast majority of the Premier League’s 115 charges of breaching financial rules.

Related: Scale of City’s punishment is the only story but Premier League must bear some responsibility | Barney Ronay

Soriano’s willingness to address the guilty verdict against City, which first emerged on Friday but has yet to be confirmed publicly by the club or the Premier League, surprised other members of the EFC board, which includes two domestic rivals in Jean-Claude Blanc, the head of Ineos Sport and chief of international football relations at Manchester United, and the Everton owner, Dan Friedkin.

Soriano is understood to have addressed the board at the start of the meeting by requesting permission to make a brief statement. He said he disagreed with the ruling of the commission, and that he and City were confident of eventually winning their battle. He added that while it had been eight years since the allegations of financial misconduct were first made against City, a definitive conclusion to the saga could take considerably more time.

Other clubs remain frustrated by the ongoing delay, saying they are being kept in the dark over the details of the case and the likely timeframe for any resolution. Club executives received a broad outline of the independent commission’s findings against City last Thursday, but there has been no update since, and the verdict has yet to be published. One club source said on Monday: ‘All we have is a void, and it would be better for everyone if it was filled as soon as possible.’

Soriano declined to comment when approached by reporters after the EFC board meeting.

The Premier League has not commented, nor given any indication of when the judgment will be published.
output.standfirst:
• Rival Premier League clubs step up calls to publish Manchester City’s verdict

  • Ferran Soriano says City will fight the ruling after being found guilty on the vast majority of the Premier League’s 115 financial charges
output.progress: Rival clubs are pressing the Premier League to publish the verdict quickly, while Ferran Soriano insists Manchester City will contest it in full.

output.headline: Merseyside fire service urges battery safety checks after fatal house blaze
output.bodyHtml:
Firefighters in Merseyside have identified a lithium-ion battery as the cause of a fire that left a mother and her three children dead.

Merseyside fire and rescue service said an electrical event caused the battery, of a type commonly used in vapes, ebikes and e-scooters, to go into “thermal runaway”.

Kevin Johnson, the fire service’s head of prevention, said: “We’re urging people to follow the manufacturer’s instructions, only using batteries and chargers which have been supplied with the vehicle or approved by the manufacturer, as anything else can pose a huge fire risk.”

Johnson said: “It’s also important to know and recognise the signs that your lithium-ion battery may be failing – if it is swelling, making unusual sounds, has a strong smell, is failing to charge or is smoking, please stop using immediately.”

Crews arrived at the blaze, which ripped through the house in Bootle, at about 3.45am on Tuesday 22 September.

Four people were discovered in an upstairs bedroom showing no signs of life, a fire service spokesperson said. North West ambulance’s hazardous area response team later confirmed that all four had died.

They were named by police as Elisha Brabin, 36, Leo Brabin, 16, Ellis Brabin, eight, and seven-year-old Prudence Brabin.

At the fire’s height, six crews were on the scene and eight firefighters entered the house.

Johnson said: “This is a devastating incident and our thoughts are very much with the family and friends of the mother and children who lost their lives and those who were injured.”

“This tragedy highlights the very real risks posed by lithium-ion batteries, which we confirmed as the source of the fire.”

The service did not confirm what the lithium-ion battery at the home was being used for.

In a tribute issued on Wednesday, relatives of the victims said: “Elisha was our beloved daughter, wife, mother, sister, aunty, niece and cousin. She was a devoted and loving mother who lived for her children. They were her whole world, and she meant everything to us.”

“Our beautiful babies, Leo, Ellis and Prudence, were loved beyond measure and brought so much joy, happiness and love to our family. They filled our lives with laughter and precious memories that we will cherish for ever.”

“The tragic loss of Elisha and our three precious children has left us heartbroken. They have all been taken from us far too soon. The loss we are experiencing is unimaginable, and the impact on our family will be felt for ever.”
output.standfirst: Merseyside fire and rescue service is urging people to check lithium-ion batteries for signs of failure, after the battery caused a blaze that killed a mother and her three children in Bootle.
output.progress: Merseyside fire and rescue service is urging people to check lithium-ion batteries for signs of failure and use only approved chargers.

output.headline: Michael Wynn-Jones, Delia Smith’s husband and Norwich City life president, dies aged 85
output.bodyHtml:
Michael Wynn-Jones, the journalist and husband of the TV chef Delia Smith, has died at the age of 85.

Wynn-Jones was honorary life president of Norwich City football club, which said everyone at the club was ‘deeply saddened’ by his death.

The club said in a statement: ‘Michael died peacefully at home on Monday morning, aged 85. He will be greatly missed. His family are grateful for the wonderful care provided by the community nursing team at St Elizabeth hospice in Ipswich.

‘Our deepest condolences are with Delia and Tom [Smith, the couple’s nephew], and with all of Michael’s family, friends and loved ones. At the family’s request, we ask that their privacy be respected at this difficult time.’

Wynn-Jones lived with Smith near Stowmarket in Suffolk and they had been married for more than 50 years.

The couple oversaw several promotions to the Premier League for the Canaries, putting the club on a solid financial footing. Smith had the more prominent, public role at Norwich City, while Wynn-Jones was reportedly regarded as a trusted adviser and influential figure in the boardroom.

Darren Huckerby, a former player for the club, posted a tribute saying Wynn-Jones ‘stayed out of the limelight but all at Norwich City FC owe him so much’.

Wynn-Jones worked as a journalist for titles including the Daily Mirror and the Spectator and founded his own publishing company.

He began attending Norwich City games in April 1955 at the age of 13. He wrote fondly of the club’s unlikely run to the FA Cup semi-final in 1959.

Norwich City Fans Social Club said in a statement: ‘All of us at NCFSC are devastated to hear the news about Michael Wynn-Jones passing. Michael is a true NCFC legend and what he did for the club cannot be underestimated. We are thinking of Delia, Tom and all of Michael’s family at this incredibly sad time. Rest in peace, Michael.’

Delia Smith previously told BBC Radio 4’s Desert Island Discs that she and Wynn-Jones bonded over their passion for food and football.

She said in 2021 she rarely cooked at home, leaving Wynn-Jones to hover over the stove while she went ‘to the end of the garden’.
output.standfirst: The former journalist and honorary life president of Norwich City died peacefully at home on Monday, having overseen the club’s rise to the Premier League alongside his wife.

output.trail: The US-owned firm's profits have doubled, with average monthly users at its UK arm surging to nearly 700,000 and sales up by a third.
